newsitem.title: BELARUS: Belarus leader warns government over inflation.
newsitem.headline: Belarus leader warns government over inflation.

text.p: President Alexander Lukashenko of Belarus warned government ministers on Tuesday to shape up or face the sack after a big jump in inflation.

Lukashenko, whose authoritarian approach has drawn criticism at home and abroad, had decreed that on average prices should grow by two percent a month this year. But in January monthly inflation stood at 13.3 percent.
"I am hearing for the first time that you have not fulfilled the programme. You have failed me!" he declared after acting prime minister Sergei Ling announced inflation data.
One independent analyst, on hearing of Lukashenko's reaction, said: "That's a bit like a bad table tennis player blaming the table."
Prices grew by 7.4 percent in December giving an average monthly increase of 2.8 percent for the whole year, but economists said the jump was at least partly seasonal.
Part of the rise was due to a liberalisation in prices and a 40 percent rise in wages and pensions since December but monetary policies were also to blame, they said.

They say Lukashenko should free exchange rates -- held until recently in a corridor but now fixed at 20,050 Belarussian roubles per dollar and well below the traded rate in Moscow -- and instigate reforms.
Ling promised to keep inflation under control by regulating prices in energy, transport and "communal services" such as rent and heating.
The two men were speaking at a cabinet meeting filmed by state television and monitored by Reuters.
Speakers faced regular interruptions and comments from the 42-year-old leader whose stop-start attitude to reforms has led to international lending bodies suspending credits.
Lukashenko, frequently mopping his brow with a handkerchief and not smiling once, spoke for more than an hour in a speech delivered in a highly disciplinarian tone.
"You have your jobs. Now do them!" he said, adding he had done his part by picking the best team from what was available.
"If the programme cannot be fulfilled, then the team will not be," he declared, making clear that ministers had to follow his instructions or face losing their jobs.
Lukashenko has sacked, demoted or accepted the resignations of a stringsof senior and medium-level officials since winning a referendum to extend his powers last November.

Gennady Aleinikov -- the fourth central bank chief since September 1995 -- said in his debut speech that interest rates should be made more realistic, a welcome signal to independent economists who say he could become a key figure this year.
"We are intending to take another look at our interest policies...The cost of credits must be realistic," he said.
Some economists fear Aleinikov, a commercial banker, will lack clout since he has little independence from the president.
They were shocked by the sacking and arrest of the last central bank chief, Tamara Vinnikova, on charges of corruption.

Vinnikova, who had backed Lukashenko at first but later criticised his monetary policies, was credited with setting up a secondary interbank market where the country's currency could be exchanged at a more realistic rate.
Economists are anxious to see changes in monetary and exchange rate policy, described in an analysis funded by the European Union last month as having "no credibility".
